RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change.
Rationale for becoming the Department of Gender and Women's Studies instead of the Gender and Women's Studies Program Overview: In designating Gender and Women's Studies (GWS) as a "Department," URI will affirm that GWS is equal in status and importance to all other Departments at URI.
Consistent with the goals outlined in the Academic Strategic Plan (2016-2021), this change will demonstrate unequivocally URI's commitment to student success, diversity, and social justice-all at the core of GWS teaching and scholarship.
Except for being accorded equal status as a "Department," since 1972, GWS has operated just like other departments.

GWS has its own budget, "director" who participates in all chair obligations and duties, growing number of majors (45 in FY2021) and minors, TT, full-time, and joint faculty lines, an endowed chair, URI Foundation funds, student scholarships, sponsored events, and a graduate certificate program that has graduated over 30 students.
But it is time now to give GWS equal status.
The current and pressing historical issues in our society-#MeToo, #BlackLivesMatter, the 2020 Centennial of the Women's Vote, and the struggle for LGBTQ rights-make it clear that leaders must take action to create equality in their institutions.
This organization change can and will make URI a leader among its peers.
This proposed change to "Department" will be a visible declaration at URI of the equal stature it accords all of its academic units.
Insofar as human rights, equality, and anti- racism teaching and scholarship are also integral to the discipline of Gender and Women's Studies, this proposed change will recognize the crucial work GWS does at URI.
Currently, there are more than 800 GWS departments nationally, but none in RI.

As the flagship university, URI will lead in establishing the first GWS department in RI, placing URI in the good company of "aspiring to be like" institutions, the University of Delaware https://www.wgs.udel.edu/academics/wgs and the University of Virginia https://wgs.as.virginia.edu/.
Specific Outcomes and rationales: As a "Department," Gender and Women's Studies will be one among equals in the College of Arts & Sciences and at URI, and across the professions, generating the following outcomes: • Affirm the value and place of Gender and Women's Studies in a university that seeks to uphold the values of diversity, equality, antiracism, and social justice.
GWS as a discipline focuses on the teaching of human rights, LGBTQ rights, social justice, Black Lives Matter, and the Me Too Movement.
The intersectional approach central to the discipline of GWS demands and enacts the study of simultaneous oppressions related to race, class, gender, sexuality, ageism, disabilities.
This intersectional approach and pedagogy positions GWS as central to educating students to understand and 2

3 address current and future national and global historical and political crises.
GWS at URI and in the world is a leader in antiracist teaching.
The designation as Department will recognize and validate GWS's role in impacting the antiracist intellectual and cultural climate and practices at the university and beyond. • Validate and honor the interdisciplinary discipline of GWS in its own right.
URI's Academic Plan places high value on interdisciplinary work.
Gender and Women's Studies is a formal interdisciplinary field unto itself.
Scholarly journals: GWS has about 40 journals worldwide dedicated to its scholarship.
A scan of the list at the end of the Rationale reveals the vast number of interdisciplinary foci that are all considered part of GWS.
Two of the journals coming out of URI are not on the Internet search list but should be: Dignity and Journal of Feminist Scholarship.
Associations and Conferences: GWS has hundreds of gender conferences and organizations worldwide, including the National Women's Studies Association, a global organization founded in 1977 with membership in the thousands and an annual conference attended by thousands.

NWSA's stated goals speak to the interdisciplinary nature inherent to the field of Gender and Women's Studies: "to demonstrate the contributions of feminist scholarship that is comparative, global, intersectional and interdisciplinary to understandings of the arts, humanities, social sciences and sciences; and to promote synergistic relationships between scholarship, teaching and civic engagement in understandings of culture and society." Leadership in the world: UN Women, established in 2010 as a major global working group, also articulates the many disciplines and subjects that come together in GWS: Leadership and political participation; economic empowerment; ending violence against women; peace and security; humanitarian action; youth; governance and national planning; sustainable development; HIV and AIDs.

While UN Women "focuses on priority areas that are fundamental to women's equality," they also recognize that this equality "unlock[s] progress across the board." As UN Women states: "All human development and human rights issues have gender dimensions." URI is long overdue in recognizing both the rightful position and place of interdisciplinary disciplines as valid and complete in themselves, and the rightful and important role GWS plays in educating students, faculty, staff, and the world on the many ways gender matters.
On the one hand, the creation of an academic department formalizes the role and responsibility of the Chair, faculty, and affiliated faculty, institutionally strengthening the academic major and course of study.
On the other hand, designating GWS as a department validates the interdisciplinary validity of this field in its own right. • Lend more credibility for students looking to major or double major in GWS.
Students will understand their investment in GWS as a single or double major as equally validating as majoring in all other departments.

In addition, on a transcript, majoring in a "Department" rather than a "Program" may also be perceived by employers and graduate programs as more substantial and equal to majors in other "Departments." As a department, with equal recognition and validation as all other departments, socially justice-minded prospective students and young scholars whose work, teaching, and passion are grounded in gender, equal rights, and social justice work will be all the more drawn to courses and majoring or double majoring in GWS. • Enhance the connections between many URI departments and faculty involved in the study of gender, equality, and social justice.
Department designation will encourage more administrators, faculty, and students to affiliate and collaborate with GWS.
Research indicates that where an organization has status differentials, including between a "Department"' and a "Program," cross- pollination and collaboration are less likely to occur.
As the GWS Department, other departments and administrators will be inclined to take GWS more seriously and reach out more to GWS as equal stakeholders.

4 • Bring URI in line with colleges and universities around the country, including universities URI aspires to and competes with for students and faculty.
There are approximately 800 universities around the country that have acquired Department status and others, like us, are seeking it.
In RI, no other college or university currently has department designation for their GWS programs.
As a Flagship University, URI should be at least up to par with our peer or "aspiring-to-be-like" institutions. "Thinking Big," URI should strive to be a leader in education and organizational design.
In RI, especially, URI should be the first to accomplish this important goal. • Attract highly competitive and diverse faculty who wish to be part of a fully recognized "Department" rather than "Program." In promotion and tenure decisions, it is also possible that working for a "Department" will be seen as more valuable, permanent, and reputable than working for a "Program." • Create growing interest in GWS leadership.
As a Department with a "Chair" instead of a "Director," faculty might be more interested in taking on the position as "Chair" of Gender and Women's Studies. • Attract external funding.

As a Department, getting grants for an individual or a department as a whole may have more credibility than getting grants for a "Program." To external funders and reviewers, programs may appear more ad hoc and less permanent than departments.
Those seeking to support research and scholarship are likely to seek more permanent "homes" for resource allocation. • Send a powerful message to all URI alumni and to GWS alumni conveying URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's studies, including a focus on: LGBTQ rights, black lives matter, the Me Too Movement, and global human rights.
Showing alumni the unequivocal support for a Department of GWS will perhaps catalyze more gift giving, scholarships, and further endowments. • Send a powerful message of support to URI students, faculty, and staff who are women, LGBTQ, nonbinary, and males advocating for equal rights URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's issues.

DATE: July 24, 2020 TO: Margaret Benz Coordinator, Faculty Senate FROM: Linda Barrett Director, Budget and Financial Planning SUBJECT: Proposal for an Organizational change in Arts & Sciences - Gender and Women's Studies As requested in an email from Brian Krueger, Associate Dean in the College of Arts & Sciences, dated July 10, 2020, the Budget and Financial Planning Office has reviewed the submitted documents related to the proposal for an Organizational change in the department of Gender and Women's Studies program. The Budget and Financial Planning Office, including communication with Enrollment Services, concurs that the request for an organizational change related to the Gender and Women's Studies program is anticipated to have a small positive net revenue impact on the Fund 100 unrestricted budget as it has been presented. Article III, Section 7 – Ethical conduct. The people of the State of Rhode Island believe that public officials and employees must adhere to the highest standards of ethical conduct, respect the public trust and the rights of all persons, be open, accountable and responsive, avoid the appearance of impropriety and not use their position for private gain or advantage.
WHAT IS “ETHICAL” CONDUCT?

Ethics: a standard or philosophy of right and wrong human behavior based on logical reasoning So… “Ethical Conduct” is the type of behavior that a logical person would agree is the “right” thing to do under the circumstances But - People have different ideas about what makes behavior “right” or “wrong”
Ethics based on CULTURE – Many people think that whether something is “ethical” depends on the setting in which it occurs, taking into account the local culture, habits and customs.

Ethics based on CONSEQUENCES - Ethical or unethical conduct is determined by examining the results. Ethical conduct is behavior that results in more positive results than negative results, in quantity and quality.

Ethics based on CHARACTER - Ethical conduct is determined by asking, “What would a virtuous person do under the circumstances?” The focus is on one’s character and motives. I am an honest, upstanding person, so how could I violate the Code of Ethics?

Focus on your ACTION, not the result ! ! ! The Code of Ethics tells us what actions to avoid, without regard to culture, consequence, or character. Ethical or unethical conduct is determined NOT by looking at the results, but at the conduct itself and judging its inherent rightness or wrongness.
Who is subject to the Code of Ethics? All elected and appointed officials and employees of state and local government, boards, commissions and agencies shall be subject to the Code of Ethics.

A person subject to the Code of Ethics . . . may not participate in any matter in which he or she has an interest, financial or otherwise, which is in substantial conflict with the proper discharge of his or her duties in the public interest. A substantial conflict of interest occurs if it is reasonably foreseeable that he or she or any family member or business associate, or any business by which he or she is employed or represents, will derive a direct monetary gain or suffer a direct monetary loss by reason of his or her official activity.

Reasonably foreseeable The conflict need not be certain to occur, but the probability must be greater than “conceivably.” Business Associates Your “business associates” are any persons or entities that you are joined with to achieve a common financial objective. These include not only your business partners, but also people you have hired such as an attorney, accountant, realtor, contractor, etc. These also include any businesses or organizations, even if not-for-profit, for which you are an officer or serve on the Board of Directors.

A conflict of interest is a situation where a person’s public duties impact, or involve, his or her private life. ► It is not unethical to have a conflict of interest. ► It does not violate the Code of Ethics to have a conflict of interest. ► It is not the conflict that is the problem; rather, the potential problem is in a failure to identify and manage the conflict.

Do I have a conflict of interest? Ask yourself . . . Is it “reasonably foreseeable” that: A decision I am helping to make as part of my public duties, will result in a financial benefit or detriment to: Me; or My family or household member; or My outside employer; or My business associate?

Ask yourself: Even if there is no financial impact, is a family member, household member, employer or business associate a party to, or participating in, the matter being discussed? If the answer is “Yes,” then you have a conflict of interest and you must recuse from any participation in the matter.

HOW TO RECUSE 1. Complete a Statement of Conflict of Interest form. 2. Present the original to your presiding officer, appointing authority, director, or immediate supervisor. 3. Send a copy to the Ethics Commission.

Nepotism - You may not participate in any matter as part of your public duties if there is reason to believe or expect that any person within your family or a household member . . . • is a party to or participant in such matter; or • will derive a direct monetary gain; or • will suffer a direct monetary loss; or • obtain an employment advantage.

These prohibitions apply regardless of whether a family or household member is objectively the most qualified candidate for a job, or is deserving of promotion. The policy underlying the prohibitions against nepotism in the Code recognizes that it is difficult for any person to be truly objective when considering matters impacting family/household members and, additionally, furthers the constitutionally founded goal of avoiding the appearance of impropriety.
